previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for her third cycle of high-dose methotrexate for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with CNS involvement. She tolerated the chemotherapy well and cleared the drug within 48 hours. During the admission, she developed abdominal pain and increased ostomy output, prompting imaging and stool studies. A CT scan showed bowel wall edema and pneumatosis, and a stool test confirmed Clostridium difficile infection, for which she was treated with oral vancomycin. Her symptoms resolved by discharge. Her diabetes was managed with insulin due to elevated blood sugars in the hospital, though she was not discharged on insulin due to hypoglycemia risk. She received IVIG for CVID and completed a dose of Neupogen to support white blood cell recovery. She was discharged home with follow-up arranged and instructions to complete her vancomycin course.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old female with a history of type 2 diabetes, common 
variable immunodeficiency on chronic IVIG since ___, chronic 
back pain, and primary colonic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma s/p 
small bowel resection with CNS involvement with recent C. diff 
infection on previous hospitalization, now presenting for 
high-dose MTX #4 for CNS lymphoma.
.
#. Primary colonic DLBCL: Admitted for MTX infusion cycle #4.  
Previously complicated by mucositis (cycle #1), so lower dose 
was given once again.  A pre-infusion CXR ruled out pleural 
effusions and maintenance fluids with NaHCO3 was given to keep 
urine pH >7, with frequent checks.  Methotrexate levels were 
monitored at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-infusion and decreased 
accordingly s/p infusion.  Leucovorin rescuse was given starting 
24 hours s/p MTX infusion.  The patient developed mild mucositis 
that was controlled with caphasol and Gelclair.  We felt there 
was an element of candidiasis to her oral lesions, so she was 
started on Fluconazole and will continue on this 
prophylactically as an outpatient.
.
#. C. diff and electrolyte abnormalities: She was previous 
discharged with PO Vancomycin for known C. diff positivity.  Her 
diarrhea had slowed down as an outpatient and she continued to 
take the Vancomycin as prescribed.  However, flatus and 
increased stool output complicated her hospital visit, but she 
found that taking Bean-o (as she had at home) was more effective 
than simethicone.  Her stools were ""foamy"" so stool studies were 
sent and returned negative.  She was also given a 3-day course 
of rifaximin to try control bacterial overgrowth secondary to 
hyperglycemia and short-gut.  She was continued on Vanc PO 125mg 
PO q6h for the duration of her stay and will continue on this at 
the discretion of her outpatient providers, instead of 14-day 
course.  Due to high ostomy output, K+ and Mg+ were repleted 
aggressively and she was sent home with supplementation.  IVF 
was continued as above to prevent dehydration
.
#. t2DM and hyperglycemia: At home, her diabetes is usually 
well-controlled with only metformin and diet.  While an 
inpatient, we held her metformin and started an ISS while in 
house.  She required 20 units of Lantus and an aggressive ISS in 
order to control her sugars, since we felt that it was more 
important for her to eat what she wanted due to her cachexia, 
than to restrict her to a diabetic diet.  Her FSBGs ran in the 
high 200s to 300s consistently, but she assured us that she 
would eat healthier and take her blood sugars often upon 
discharge.
.
#. Chronic back pain: Patient has back and leg pain all of the 
time and is managed with a regimen of medications that seems to 
keep her pain under control.  She was continued on methadone, 
oxycodone, and cyclobenzaprine.
.
#. Follow-up:  Her pentamidine PCP prophylaxis will be due as an 
outpatient on ___ (given last on ___.  She will also likely 
need IVIG as outpatient in the near future for her 
immunodeficiency.  She was provided only with a week's worth of 
narcotics and benzos and an e-mail was sent to her PCP, the 
purveyor of her narcotics contract.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___, 
It was a pleasure taking part in your care at the ___ 
___.  You were admitted for a cycle of 
methotrexate chemotherapy and monitored  for a number of days.  
Your diarrhea, likely caused by your previous C.difficile 
infection, continued and you also had a fungal infection in your 
mouth that we treated with an anti-fungal medication.  There may 
have been an element of mucositis that we treated with routine 
oral care medications and pain medications as needed.  Your 
blood sugars were high during your stay, so we started you on 
standing long-acting insulin daily along with extra insulin 
during the day if you blood sugar was too high.  Your 
methotrexate blood levels decreased appropriately and you were 
discharged with close follow-up with your primary oncology team. 
 

We have made the following changes in your medications:
1) START fluconazole for protection against fungal infections 
when your cell counts are low
2) START acyclovir for protection against viral infections when 
your cell counts are low
3) START caphasol as needed for your mucositis 
4) START potassium chloride supplements to help replace the 
potassium in your blood
5) START magnesium oxide to help replaced the magnesium in your 
blood
